title: API 510 Training in Philadelphia: Pressure Vessel Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Delaware Valley vessel inspectors at Trainer, Marcus Hook, Paulsboro and Delaware City, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Philadelphia: Exam Preparation for Pressure Vessel Inspectors on the Delaware River, from Trainer to Delaware City
html:
API 510 exam prep for pressure vessel inspectors around Philadelphia

Most of the pressure vessels a Philadelphia inspector looks after are not in the city at all. They stand along the tidal Delaware: at the Monroe Energy refinery in Trainer, in the gas-liquids complex at Marcus Hook, across the river at Paulsboro and downstream at Delaware City, with chemical plants and terminals between them. This page is for the owner-user inspectors, contract inspectors, NDT technicians and engineers who inspect those columns, drums, reactors and exchanger shells and want API 510 certification behind their signature.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia. The API 510 course is self-paced and online, and an instructor answers your questions while you study, so it fits around a rotating shift in Trainer. Eligibility is decided by the American Petroleum Institute, which administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification. The course prepares you for that examination; it is not a certification, and Atlantis holds no API training-provider approval.

Three refineries within reach of Center City, in EIA’s figures

The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Refinery Capacity Report, which gives each plant’s position at the start of 2026, lists three operating refineries within about an hour of Philadelphia. Monroe Energy, which EIA lists under Delta Air Lines, runs the Trainer refinery in Delaware County; Delta described it in 2012 as about 10 miles south-west of downtown Philadelphia. PBF Energy owns the other two, Paulsboro Refining Co. in Gloucester County, New Jersey, and Delaware City Refining Co. in Delaware. Crude distillation below is in barrels per calendar day; the other rows are in barrels per stream day, except hydrogen (million cubic feet a day) and sulfur (short tons a day).

Read each row as a family of vessels. Catalytic cracking means a reactor, regenerator, main fractionator and gas-plant towers; fluid coking, listed only at Delaware City, adds a reactor and burner in hot, erosive service. Hydrocracking and hydrotreating mean thick-walled reactors and high-pressure separators in hydrogen service, and the sulfur row hints at how many amine regenerators, sour water strippers and sulfur recovery vessels a site keeps. Paulsboro’s profile is different: EIA lists no catalytic cracker there but does list asphalt and lubricant production, and PBF describes the plant as a maker of Group I lubricant base oils.

Two sites matter for what they no longer do. EIA lists the CPI Operations refinery at Paulsboro as idle, and PBF now describes that site as marine, railcar, asphalt and storage infrastructure. The large South Philadelphia refinery no longer refines either: about 1,300 acres of it are being redeveloped by HRP Group as the Bellwether District, where The Philadelphia Inquirer reported in November 2025 that a first warehouse was finished and a second was nearing completion.

Gas liquids at Marcus Hook and chemical vessels inside the city

On the Delaware state line, Energy Transfer’s Marcus Hook complex occupies a former Sunoco refinery that was idled in 2011. A company fact sheet posted by Pennsylvania’s Department of Environmental Protection in 2023 lists the units built for the Mariner East project: an ethane/propane splitter, ethane and propane chilling, refrigerated storage, and a fractionator for gas liquids that arrive from western Pennsylvania on the Mariner East pipelines. For an API 510 candidate that means columns and drums in light-hydrocarbon service, chillers running far below ambient, and a recurring question about whether carbon steel can fall below its minimum design metal temperature during depressurisation. Large chilled storage tanks follow low-temperature tank standards rather than Section VIII; the pressurised drums, towers and exchanger shells around them are vessel work.

Inside the city, AdvanSix runs its Frankford plant, which has its own Delaware River dock and which the company describes as one of North America’s largest producers of phenol. The site also makes acetone and alpha-methylstyrene and sends phenol to the company’s Hopewell, Virginia, plant to make caprolactam. Its reactors, columns and exchangers are a reminder that API 510 covers chemical plants as fully as refineries.

Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware: whose vessel law applies

Within 30 miles of Philadelphia a vessel inspector can work in three states, each with its own boiler and pressure vessel law. The API 510 certificate means the same in all three; the jurisdictional credentials do not.

StateLaw and administratorWhat the jurisdiction expects
PennsylvaniaBoiler and Unfired Pressure Vessel Law (Act 85 of 1998, amended by Act 104 of 2013) and 34 Pa. Code Chapter 3a, run by the Department of Labor & Industry’s Boiler DivisionUnfired pressure vessels inspected every 36 months, with an internal inspection when the inspector requires one because of age or condition. The inspector holds a current Pennsylvania commission, for which a National Board commission card is required; owners may have their own employees commissioned for vessels in process operations.
New JerseyMechanical Inspection Bureau of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Compliance, Department of Labor and Workforce Development; discharge-prevention rules for major facilities in N.J.A.C. 7:1EOnly the bureau inspects new or replacement equipment; the owner then chooses the state or an authorized insurance company inspector for later inspections, and a pressure vessel owner-user can run an in-house programme by qualifying as an Owner-User Inspection Organization under N.J.A.C. 12:90-5.19. Field-erected pressure tanks over 2,000 gallons at major facilities may not use API 510’s similar-service or risk-based scheduling.
DelawareBoiler Safety Program under 7 Del. C. Chapter 74B and 7 DE Admin. Code 1353, part of DNREC’s Division of Waste and Hazardous SubstancesRegistration and inspection of boilers and pressure vessels, with reports of inspection from an inspector commissioned by the National Board or by Delaware.

Two further Pennsylvania details come up on Delaware County sites: the Boiler Division issues a certificate of operation after inspection and a copy has to be posted where it can be seen, and welded repairs and alterations may be made only by holders of the National Board R stamp, working to the National Board Inspection Code.

Inside the city limits one more layer concerns people rather than vessels: the Philadelphia Code requires a Department of Licenses and Inspections licence to operate or maintain a steam or high-temperature hot water boiler. None of these credentials is an API 510 certificate, and the API exam asks nothing about them. Atlantis’s page on API 510 vessel inspection in Pennsylvania looks at the same law from the owner’s side.

Damage a Delaware Valley vessel inspector learns to expect

The river sets much of the damage picture. The Delaware River Basin Commission places the average position of the salt front, where chloride reaches 250 mg/L, around Wilmington, and it warns that salty water can corrode industrial intakes and other infrastructure. Delaware City lies downstream of that average, so river water drawn there is brackish; Trainer and Marcus Hook are usually upstream, although the front reached river mile 89, near Philadelphia International Airport, in the 2002 drought. For API 510 work that means the water side of exchangers: chloride pitting of channels and shells, under-deposit attack and microbiologically influenced corrosion, all in API RP 571.

Crude quality is the second driver. PBF says Delaware City can process a diverse heavy slate with a high concentration of high-sulfur crudes, which points the inspection plan at sulfidation in hot crude and vacuum equipment, wet hydrogen sulfide damage in sour water and amine vessels, and high temperature hydrogen attack screening for hydroprocessing reactors and their exchangers. At Marcus Hook the lead concern is toughness rather than thinning, so brittle fracture is the RP 571 mechanism a candidate from there should know best.

Then there is the weather. The National Weather Service’s normals for Philadelphia International Airport give a January normal low of 26°F, so water trapped in a bottom head or an idle exchanger can freeze, and wet insulation stays wet for months. Corrosion under insulation is not only a piping topic here; insulated shells, nozzles and skirts need the same attention.

Worked example: the bottom head of a water knockout drum

Exam questions often hide the difficulty in the bottom head, where standing liquid adds to the pressure. Take a vertical knockout drum with a 2:1 ellipsoidal bottom head of 60 in. inside diameter. The head is seamless, and the question sets its joint efficiency E at 1.0 (for seamless heads Section VIII decides E under UW-12(d)). Design pressure at the top of the drum is 150 psi, water can stand 10 ft above the bottom head, and the question gives the allowable stress S as 20,000 psi. Section VIII, Division 1 gives the required thickness of a 2:1 ellipsoidal head as t = PD ÷ (2SE − 0.2P).

  1. Pressure at the head. The API 510 Body of Knowledge bases static head on a specific gravity of 1.0, which is 0.433 psi per foot, so the bottom head sees 150 + 10 × 0.433 = 154.3 psi.
  2. Required thickness. t = 154.3 × 60 ÷ (40,000 − 30.9) = 9,258 ÷ 39,969 = 0.232 in.
  3. Corrosion rates. The lowest reading in the bottom head was 0.332 in. at the inspection 12 years ago, 0.310 in. six years ago and 0.284 in. today. Long-term rate: 0.048 ÷ 12 = 0.0040 in. per year. Short-term rate: 0.026 ÷ 6 = 0.0043 in. per year. API 510 asks for the rate that best reflects current conditions; with no sign the process has improved, use the higher short-term rate.
  4. Remaining life. (0.284 − 0.232) ÷ 0.0043 = about 12.1 years.
  5. Next internal inspection. Unless an RBI assessment justifies something else, API 510 caps the internal or on-stream interval at half the remaining life or 10 years, whichever is less, so this head sets an interval of about 6 years.
  6. MAWP for continued service. API 510 does not rate the head on today’s reading: the thickness used is the measured thickness minus twice the corrosion expected before the next inspection, here 0.284 − 2 × 6 × 0.0043 = 0.232 in. The head’s MAWP is then 2SEt ÷ (D + 0.2t) = 40,000 × 0.232 ÷ 60.05 = about 154.5 psi at the head, which is about 150 psi at the top of the drum once the 4.3 psi of static head is taken off.

That last result is no coincidence: an interval of half the remaining life means twice the expected loss uses up exactly the corrosion allowance that is left. The traps are forgetting the static head, taking the long-term rate because it is kinder, subtracting the corrosion loss only once in the MAWP check, and quoting the bottom head’s own MAWP as the vessel’s, which Section VIII sets at the top of the vessel. The head formula belongs to the open-book half, where you will find it in the Section VIII PDF; the interval rule and the choice of corrosion rate are API 510 knowledge you should carry into the closed-book half. Check each clause in the edition on your window’s Publications Effectivity Sheet. More of the same is on the API 510 practice questions page.

Routes into API 510 from Philadelphia-area jobs

API counts experience from the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency, and less is needed as education rises. Common local starting points:

  • Engineering graduates. With a BS in engineering or technology, API asks for one year spent supervising or performing the inspection work API 510 describes. Widener University’s ABET-accredited chemical engineering programme in Chester, a short drive from Trainer, is one local source of candidates on this shortest route.
  • NDT technicians. Contract UT, MT, PT and VT technicians on Delaware Valley turnarounds already perform inspection activities. With a two-year technical degree the requirement is two years, with a high-school diploma three. Atlantis offers ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT training for Philadelphia for those still building the method side.
  • Boilermakers and pipefitters. Energy Transfer’s fact sheet records a project labour agreement with the Philadelphia Building Trades for work at Marcus Hook. Vessel repair and construction experience counts on the longer routes if at least one year involved supervising or performing inspection.
  • Operators and licensed boiler engineers. Operating experience with pressure vessels counts on the two-, three- and five-year routes, again including a year of inspection.
  • Welding inspectors. A welding inspector who already reviews procedures and repairs is close to much of the API 510 repair content; Atlantis also runs AWS CWI exam prep for Philadelphia.

API, not Atlantis, verifies the experience on each application. The API 510 certification requirements page sets out the routes in full.

Fitting API 510 study around Delaware Valley turnarounds and winters

Turnarounds and outdoor work in the Delaware Valley tend to bunch into the milder months, so inspection staff often face busy springs and autumns and quieter winters. A self-paced course lets you study hard when it is quiet and slowly when a turnaround takes over. Choose an exam window that falls after your busiest outage rather than in the middle of it, apply to API before that window’s deadline, and keep your study plan pointed at the Publications Effectivity Sheet for the window you have chosen.

Use the outage too. A turnaround puts heads, nozzles, internals, repair plans and pressure tests in front of you; send the questions they raise to the instructor, who answers from the code text. The examination is taken in person, and Prometric lists test centres in and around Philadelphia; book early in the window if you need a particular day.

Other ways to prepare in Philadelphia, compared fairly

  • Classroom exam-prep courses. Training companies run intensive classroom courses on fixed dates, usually away from home; they suit people who want a set timetable and can be released from work.
  • Employer in-house programmes. A refinery or terminal operator may coach its own candidates with site examples. That builds judgement but may not follow the Body of Knowledge closely.
  • Self-study from the code books. Cheapest, but there is no one to ask when a calculation will not close.
  • A self-paced online course with instructor Q&A. The format Atlantis offers: it fits shift work, but you have to keep yourself going.

Sponsoring API 510 candidates from a Delaware Valley site

An owner or inspection company with people at Trainer, Paulsboro and Delaware City can send them all through one enquiry and one quote, even though each candidate studies on a separate timetable and may sit a different window. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate still applies to API individually and is assessed on their own experience, so check eligibility before enrolling anyone.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 class I can attend in person in Philadelphia?
faq.a: Not with Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in Philadelphia, and the API 510 course is self-paced online study with instructor Q&A, so you start when you enrol and study around your shifts. The examination itself is the in-person part: API administers it at Prometric test centres, and Prometric lists centres in and around Philadelphia. Book your seat as soon as API accepts your application for the window.

faq.q: Does a Pennsylvania boiler inspector commission replace API 510 certification?
faq.a: No. The Pennsylvania commission lets you make jurisdictional inspections under the Boiler and Unfired Pressure Vessel Law, and it requires a National Board commission card. API 510 certification shows command of the in-service inspection code that refiners and chemical plants use to run their vessel programmes. Many owner-user inspectors in the region carry both, and the API course prepares you only for the API examination.

faq.q: I hold a City of Philadelphia boiler operator licence. Does that experience count toward API 510?
faq.a: It may help, but probably not on its own. API counts design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels on the two-, three- and five-year routes, and at least one year must be supervision or performance of inspection. Boiler operation is not the same as pressure vessel inspection, so describe any vessel work precisely on your application. API verifies the experience and makes the decision.

faq.q: Is the chilled gas-liquids storage at Marcus Hook API 510 equipment?
faq.a: Large chilled storage tanks for propane, ethane or butane are designed to low-temperature tank standards rather than Section VIII, so they are not the core of API 510. The pressurised drums, splitter and fractionator columns, chillers and exchanger shells around them are pressure vessels, and their in-service inspection is API 510 work. The distinction is worth getting right when you describe your experience to API.

faq.q: I graduated in chemical engineering from Widener. When can I sit API 510?
faq.a: A bachelor’s degree in engineering or technology needs one year of experience in supervising or performing inspection activities as described in API 510, gained within the last 10 years while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. Co-op time may or may not qualify, depending on what you did; API decides when it reviews your application.

faq.q: Does the API 510 exam test Pennsylvania’s 36-month vessel inspection rule?
faq.a: No. The examination tests API 510 and the documents on the Publications Effectivity Sheet for your window, such as Section VIII and the API recommended practices. State and city rules decide how you work in the Delaware Valley, but when you practise, answer strictly from the code, because an answer based on Pennsylvania law will be marked wrong.
